summary: Internationalized domain names let DNS zones allow a huge range of Unicode characters, but most zone operators should not permit all of them. This memo sets out principles for deciding whether a Unicode code point is safe to include in the labels a zone accepts. It matters most for zones taking registrations from others, such as top-level domains and the root. The authors note that no algorithm can settle this automatically.

plainLanguage.summary: A huge box of letters from every language is available for website names, but some look alike and cause trouble. This guide helps the people who run name lists pick which letters are safe to allow.

questions: which unicode characters should be allowed in domain names
how to decide which code points are safe for dns
subtitle: Guidelines for deciding which Unicode characters are safe in domain names

tldr.problem: Internationalized domain names (IDNA) make a vast range of Unicode characters available for domain names, but most zone operators should not permit all of them. The challenge is determining which characters are safe without an algorithmic rule, especially in shared zones like the root.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6912 presents principles for zone operators to guide their code point policies: longevity (stable Unicode properties), least astonishment (matching user expectations), conservatism (preferring to exclude risky characters), and simplicity (rules that experts can understand and apply consistently).
tldr.outcome: Different zones apply different rules: zones shared across the internet (especially the root) use many principles and are highly restrictive, while private zones can be more permissive. The RFC is informational guidance from the Internet Architecture Board, not a protocol standard.

today: RFC 6912 is an informational IAB document that has not been obsoleted. It provides guidance that zone operators continue to use when establishing policies for internationalized domain names.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
The IDNA protocol allows thousands of Unicode code points in domain name labels. However, some characters look visually identical or confusingly similar (for example, a Cyrillic letter that looks like a Latin letter), and some vary in meaning between languages or contexts. An algorithm cannot determine safety; experts must decide case by case based on principles.

RFC 6912 explains that no single algorithm exists or could exist to determine which code points are safe, even though many communities across computer science have grappled with similar problems. The RFC therefore provides meta-rules: principles to guide the decision-making process itself.
sections.plainLanguage: You cannot write a program to say which letters are safe because the answer depends on language, context, and what people expect. Instead, the RFC gives principles for people to use when deciding.

sections.title: Universal Principles
sections.content: Three principles apply to every DNS zone. The Longevity Principle requires that Unicode properties stay stable across Unicode versions that users are likely to have installed. The Least Astonishment Principle asks zone administrators to consider what characters a user community expects: including characters normal in a language is good, but excluding them can be surprising. The Contextual Safety Principle requires sensitivity to visual confusion and malicious use: even a digit 1 and lowercase L are easily confused in many fonts.
sections.plainLanguage: Every zone should check that letters have stable meanings, should not surprise the people using the zone, and should watch for characters that look alike or could be used for tricks.

sections.title: Public Zone Principles
sections.content: Five additional principles apply to DNS zones that accept registrations from outside organizations, including the root zone. The Conservatism Principle says when in doubt, exclude a character. The Inclusion Principle flips the default: code points should be excluded unless proven safe. The Simplicity Principle requires rules simple enough that domain experts can understand and remember them. The Predictability Principle seeks rules that experts applying professional judgment will consistently apply the same way. The Stability Principle recognizes that once a code point is permitted, removing it later is nearly impossible, so the list should change very slowly, if at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Shared zones need stricter rules. Characters should be excluded by default, included only when proven safe, with simple rules that experts apply the same way, and seldom changed once decided.

sections.title: The Root Zone Letter Principle
sections.content:
The root zone—the authoritative database of all top-level domains—should follow the Letter Principle: code points that are not normally used to write words, or are normally used for other purposes, should be excluded. This is stricter than Unicode's letter categories. For example, marks that are used to write words in languages like Indic languages may be included, but marks used for music notation should not be, even though both have mark category values.

The RFC emphasizes this should be applied narrowly: the goal is not to exclude all non-letters, but to exclude code points used for specialized purposes outside the normal writing of words.
sections.plainLanguage: In the main list of all top-level domains, only add code points that are normally used to write words, not symbols, marks for special purposes, or characters used for music or math.

sections.title: Focus on Label Confusability
sections.content: Instead of analyzing individual characters for confusability, the RFC recommends focusing on whether one label (domain name component) is confusable with another. A label with several characters from a single script—all distinct and all from that script—is inherently safe from confusion with labels from other scripts, even if individual characters might be visually similar across scripts. The confusability focus moves from the character level to the label level, which is more practical and less restrictive.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of banning characters because they look like other characters, check whether whole domain names would be confused with each other. A word in Japanese is not confusable with a word in Arabic, even if a few letters might look similar.
